title: The carpenter
hookLine: Jesus is called a carpenter by his neighbors (Mark 6:3)

cards: His own country, Mark calls it. On the sabbath day a local man stands up in the synagogue to teach, and Mark's Gospel says the hearers were astonished. Where did he get all this?
Then the question comes out loud, and the King James Bible keeps it word for word: "Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary." They know him. They name his mother, his brothers, his sisters.
And because they know him, they can't hear him. Today's word is the job his neighbors gave him.

teach.b: Start with the word itself. Mark doesn't introduce Jesus as a carpenter. His neighbors do, almost as a put-down.

In Mark the line is "Is not this the carpenter." In Matthew's telling of the same scene it becomes "Is not this the carpenter's son?" So one Gospel gives the trade to Jesus, and another gives it to Joseph.
Readers have noticed the difference, and some simply hear both: a family trade, passed from father to son. Second, the silence.

teach.h: THE GOSPELS NEVER SAY WHAT HE BUILT.
teach.b: The Gospels never tell us what he built. No tables, no doorframes, no workshop scenes. The text gives one word and stops.
Third, what the neighbors do with it.
Mark says, "they were offended at him." Familiar hands, an ordinary trade, and so the wisdom can't be real. Jesus answers: "A prophet is not without honour, but in his own country."
Christians say Jesus is God made flesh, and some find meaning in the fact that, before any teaching, he had a trade, and he worked with his hands.
Catholics honor Joseph with a feast of St Joseph the Worker.

Whatever a listener believes about Jesus, the word sits there as a quiet challenge: the people who build and fix and carry are easy to look past, the way his neighbors looked past the wisdom to the trade.

how: Christians read Mark 6 as part of the Gospel, and some churches hold prayers or blessings for workers; Catholics keep a feast of St Joseph the Worker.

o: a Gospel name for Joseph, never for Jesus himself

s: the Gospels describe the things Jesus built

Mark says the carpenter; Matthew says the carpenter's son.
the hometown crowd welcomed his teaching
Mark says they were offended at him.

games.q: you're in the Nazareth synagogue. the local carpenter you've known for years stands up and teaches with startling wisdom. what does the crowd do?
o: they ask him to stay and teach every sabbath.
they're offended: they know his trade and his family.
they leave quietly and say nothing.
games.why: Mark says they were offended at him. knowing him as the carpenter made it hard to hear him, and he answered: a prophet is not without honour, but in his own country.

practice: Look around, or picture the room: someone built the chair under you, laid the floor, ran the wires, stitched the clothes you're wearing.
Pick one of them, a person whose name you'll never know, and picture their hands at work, the dust, the ache at the end of the day; breathe in what they made possible for you, and breathe out thanks.
If you pray, you can hold that worker in your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: The carpenter. What his hometown called Jesus when it couldn't believe the wisdom coming from a man who worked with his hands. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: easy to look past. Someone's hands built the room you're in. That's day eight hundred eighty-seven.
